title: “I Love Lucy” … in the Kitchen
content:
—This is a guest post by Ellie Hart, an archives processing technician in the Music Division. It also appears in the November/December issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.

Many fans know the “Pioneer Women” episode of “I Love Lucy” where Lucy and Ethel overzealously knead a ball of dough and accidentally bake a loaf of bread the size of a sofa. The real-life Lucille Ball and husband Desi Arnaz — a quintessential 1950s showbiz couple — were far more capable in the kitchen than that comic disaster suggests.

The Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz Papers, part of the collections of the Library’s Music Division, contain two cookbooks plus a cheerful jumble of loose recipes and notes — handwritten, typed or torn from magazines and newspapers — that demonstrate their skill with a skillet.

Their copy of “The Settlement” cookbook is peppered with handwritten notes by Lucille and Desi in the margins. Their own homemade, unpublished cookbook — in a volume emblazoned “Cash” — is filled with page after page of handwritten recipes for favorite dishes: stuffed bell peppers, light tea cake, persimmon cake, cheese blintzes.

title: How Stanley Kubrick Got His Start
content:
If Stanley Kubrick had not become one of the 20th century’s most influential film directors, there’s no doubt he would have become a highly successful photographer, perhaps even one of the century’s most influential.

This bold assertion doesn’t require much of a leap, since the “Dr. Strangelove,” “2001: A Space Odyssey” and “The Shining” director sold his first photograph to Look (“America’s Family Magazine”) when he was still in high school, was hired as an apprentice at 17 and was already a highly successful staffer at 19.

The work came in place of college training, as Kubrick’s work ethic paid off in the rapid development of style, composition, lighting and a narrative eye. The photo magazine entrusted its teen star to shoot A-list movie stars and complex stories about social issues and sent him on the road to do so. Kubrick’s progression is clear in the 100 story assignments preserved at the Library in the Look Magazine Photograph Collection, with 150 of his images online in the Prints and Photographs Division. (Part of the Look archive is at the Museum of the City of New York.)
